title: The Free School and the Palace of Glass: Paxton, the Duke, and the Building That Could Not Stay
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Seventh Son: Bedfordshire and Other Men's Gardens

stops.name: Milton Bryan, the seventh son
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and place by the 1865 obituary reprinted by Bedfordshire Archives, which gives 'born at Milton Bryant, near Woburn, Bedfordshire, August 3rd 1803'. Contradiction not resolved: his own Chiswick employment record and the old Dictionary of National Biography give 1801, apparently because he overstated his age when applying. The frequently repeated 'youngest of nine children of William and Ann Paxton' is unsupported by any source reached; Wikipedia says only 'the seventh son of a farming family'.
stops.campa: A farming family at Milton Bryant, near Woburn, has another boy. The obituary printed at his death gives the day as the third of August 1803; the surviving record calls him the seventh son of a farming family and stops there, naming neither the parents nor a count of children. The land his father works is not the family's own. He will one day tell an employer he was born in 1801, and that lie outlives him, printed as fact in the reference books for eighty years.
suggested_refs: The 1865 obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton, Bedfordshire Archives, reference CRT180/89
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton' (bedsarchives.bedford.gov.uk)

stops.name: Woburn, the free school
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was educated at the Woburn free school (Bedfordshire Archives obituary); no year is given in any source reached, and the date here is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: His father dies and the family drops. What schooling he gets is the free school at Woburn, and it is the whole of the formal education of his life: no Latin, no drawing master, no articles with an architect. Everything he later builds he learns standing in wet ground with a spade in his hand. The Duke of Bedford's gardens are close enough to walk to, glasshouses and imported exotics kept behind estate walls, and a boy from a farming family sees them the way such a boy sees them, from outside.
suggested_refs: Woburn free school, Bedfordshire, the only school Paxton is recorded as attending
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

stops.name: Battlesden Park, the garden boy and the lake
stops.date_confidence: attested that he began at Battlesden under his brother John at about fifteen (Wikipedia; DNB 1885-1900), and that he returned in 1821 and built a lake there (DNB 1885-1900). Coordinate corrected: the research dossier gave 51.9591, -0.6317, about 2.9 km off; the pin here follows Wikipedia's Battlesden at approximately 51.948, -0.596.
stops.campa: At about fifteen he goes to work under his elder brother John in the gardens of Sir Gregory Page-Turner at Battlesden, a few fields from where he was born. He leaves, trains elsewhere, and comes back in 1821 as gardener in his own right, and here he is credited with digging out a large ornamental lake. That is the first item on his record that is engineering rather than horticulture: moving water, holding it, deciding where the ground ought to be lower than it is. He is eighteen years old.
suggested_refs: The lake at Battlesden Park, credited to Paxton in the Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900

stops.name: Woodhall Park, learning to force fruit
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900, which places him under William Griffin at Samuel Smith's Woodhall Park; the years c. 1819-1821 are the DNB's approximation, not a document. Coordinate corrected: the dossier gave 51.8994, -0.1349, roughly 5.2 km off, the largest error in the set; Woodhall Park near Watton-at-Stone is at approximately 51.853, -0.090.
stops.campa: In Hertfordshire, near Watton, he trains under William Griffin, head gardener to Samuel Smith at Woodhall Park and known for forcing fruit out of its season. The work is flues, frames, and glass angled at the low winter sun: the manufacture of a climate inside a box, kept up through the night by a man who has to know when to stoke and when to vent. Here the trade stops being planting and becomes building. The Dictionary of National Biography gives him about three years of it, from 1819, and does not say what he grew.
suggested_refs: William Griffin's forcing houses at Woodhall Park, Hertfordshire

stops.name: Chiswick, two years added to his age
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Horticultural Society's Chiswick entry record of 13 November 1823 carries an age two years greater than his true one, which is the documented origin of the 1801 birth year in later reference works. The eighteen shillings a week and the thought of emigration come from the DNB, 1885-1900.
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of November he enters the Horticultural Society of London's experimental garden at Chiswick as a labourer. On the entry book he gives his age as two years more than it is, and that small falsification, made by a young man who wants the place, is the reason the reference works will print his birth as 1801 long after he is dead. Within six months he is working under the superintendent Donald Munro. He earns eighteen shillings a week, and at some point in these years he considers giving it up and emigrating to America.
suggested_refs: The Horticultural Society of London's Chiswick entry register, 13 November 1823
sources: Kate Colquhoun's Chiswick study, as summarised by the Brentford and Chiswick Local History Society

stops.name: Chiswick, foreman of the arboretum
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arboretum foremanship in 1824 (DNB 1885-1900). Reconstruction for the meeting: the sources say the sixth Duke of Devonshire noticed Paxton at Chiswick, whose garden adjoined ground the Duke held, but no dated account of a first conversation survives. Month set to order the segment.
stops.campa: By 1824 he has charge of the arboretum, a living encyclopaedia of trees swollen by every plant-hunting expedition the age can finance: seed off ships from Chile, from the Himalaya, from the Pacific coast of North America. The garden backs onto ground held by William Spencer Cavendish, sixth Duke of Devonshire, unmarried, childless, and rich past reckoning, who walks through it and notices the young foreman. Paxton is twenty-two years old and has never had a household of men to run.
suggested_refs: The arboretum of the Horticultural Society garden at Chiswick, adjoining Chiswick House
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

segments.name: Chatsworth: The Duke, the Wall, and the Morning Before Nine

stops.name: Chatsworth, the first morning
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment on 9 May 1826 at age twenty-two (Bedfordshire Archives obituary; DNB 1885-1900). Tradition for the first morning: Paxton told versions of the wall-climbing story himself and Victorian obituaries repeat it, but the hour, the order of events, and the dialogue are not independently documented. The marriage to Sarah Bown in 1827 is attested.
stops.campa: He arrives to run the gardens of the sixth Duke of Devonshire at about seventy pounds a year and a cottage. The story he tells afterwards, and which the obituaries repeat, has him reaching Chatsworth before dawn, climbing the kitchen-garden wall because nobody is awake to open a gate, walking the whole ground, setting the men to work, taking breakfast with the housekeeper, and meeting her niece Sarah Bown, all of it before nine in the morning. He marries Sarah the following year. The hour and the dialogue are nobody's record but his own.
suggested_refs: The kitchen-garden wall at Chatsworth, over which Paxton said he climbed on 9 May 1826
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

stops.name: Chatsworth, the Pinetum
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia's Chatsworth House article gives the Pinetum as established in 1829 on an additional eight acres of park. Date corrected: the research dossier gave 1830-1831.
stops.campa: Eight acres of park are taken in for a pinetum, a planted collection of conifers gathered out of the era's imports and set in order so that they can be compared with one another. It is the first of the works that turn a nobleman's garden into a laboratory: not a display but an experiment with a fence round it. Trees arrive by cart from English nurseries and by ship from Asia and the Americas. The Duke pays for all of it, and will go on paying for thirty years.
suggested_refs: The Chatsworth Pinetum, eight acres taken in from the park in 1829
sources: Chatsworth House official garden history, 'The 6th Duke and Paxton' (chatsworth.org)

stops.name: Chatsworth, the magazines and the fellowships
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Horticultural Society fellowship (1826) and the Linnean Society fellowship (1833) by the Bedfordshire Archives obituary, and for Paxton's Magazine of Botany from 1834 by Wikipedia. The Horticultural Register co-founded with Joseph Harrison in 1831 is reported by Wikipedia and consistent with the obituary's account of his publishing, but no title page was inspected.
stops.campa: The head gardener becomes a publisher. With the nurseryman Joseph Harrison he starts The Horticultural Register and General Magazine, and three years later begins Paxton's Magazine of Botany and Register of Flowering Plants, an illustrated serial carrying his own name on the spine, which he edits into the 1840s. He has been a Fellow of the Horticultural Society since 1826 and is elected to the Linnean Society in 1833. No title page of the Register was inspected for this account; the founding is reported rather than seen.
suggested_refs: Paxton's Magazine of Botany and Register of Flowering Plants, 1834 onward
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

stops.name: Chatsworth, the Cavendish banana
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline: a banana plant brought from Mauritius flowered at Chatsworth in November 1835 and fruited by May 1836, and the variety was named for the Cavendish family. The reported purchase price of ten pounds and the fruit count of more than a hundred come from the Chatsworth institutional account and are reproduced as reported.
stops.campa: A banana plant reaches Chatsworth out of Mauritius, bought for the Duke at a reported ten pounds. Paxton neither bred it nor found it. He grows it under glass, it flowers in November, and by the following May it is carrying more than a hundred fruits. The variety is named for the Cavendish family, and a century on the Cavendish is most of the banana the world eats. The Horticultural Society gives him an award for the fruit. The price and the count of fruits are the Chatsworth house account's own figures.
suggested_refs: Musa cavendishii, the Chatsworth banana of 1835-1836

stops.name: Chatsworth, the Great Stove begun
stops.date_confidence: attested that construction of the Great Conservatory began in 1836 and ran roughly four years (Chatsworth official history). The eight boilers, the seven miles of pipe, and Decimus Burton's consultation come from the same institutional account; the forty miles of sash-bar and the sash-bar machine come from the 1865 obituary.
stops.campa: Work starts on the Great Conservatory and will run four years. Eight coal boilers go in underground, feeding seven miles of pipe; the sash-bars are cut by a machine Paxton invents for the purpose, forty miles of them, set ridge and furrow so that each length of glass catches the low sun and sheds its rain sideways. The architect Decimus Burton is consulted on the profile, so the building is not his alone whatever the legend afterwards says. Carriages will drive two abreast down the middle of it under palms.
stops.quote: the forty miles of sash-bar required for the conservatory were made be a machine of his own invention
stops.quote_source: Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton, 1865, as transcribed by Bedfordshire Archives (CRT180/89); the transcript reads 'made be' where 'made by' is evidently meant, and is quoted here unaltered
suggested_refs: Paxton's sash-bar cutting machine, patented device behind the ridge-and-furrow glazing
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

segments.name: The Glass Years: Chatsworth, the Parks, and the Waterlily

stops.name: The Alps, seven months with the Duke
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline only: an extended tour of roughly seven months with the sixth Duke through Switzerland, Italy, Greece, Ottoman Asia Minor, Malta, Spain and Portugal. Honest gap: no stop-by-stop itinerary survives in the sources reached, and this coordinate is a representative Alpine waypoint, not a documented halt.
stops.campa: He leaves the garden and goes travelling with his employer: some seven months through Switzerland and Italy, then Greece, Ottoman Asia Minor, Malta, Spain and Portugal, looking at gardens and estates and at the way other countries hold their water and grow their fruit. No stop-by-stop itinerary survives in the accessible papers, so the journey is documented in outline and not in sequence. He is thirty-five and has scarcely been out of England. He comes home to finish the largest glass building in the country.
suggested_refs: The Chatsworth Archives correspondence catalogue, for the sixth Duke's continental tour of 1838

stops.name: Edensor, the village rebuilt
stops.date_confidence: attested for the remodelling of Edensor in 1839-1841 under Paxton's general direction, with individual house designs by John Robertson and others (DNB 1885-1900). Coordinate corrected: the dossier gave 53.2247, -1.6154; Edensor sits at approximately 53.227, -1.625.
stops.campa: The Duke wants the village out of his sightline and made picturesque, and Paxton directs the rebuilding: Italianate, Swiss, Norman, Tudor, no two houses alike, set out on a slope above the park. The individual designs come from the architect John Robertson and others working to Paxton's general scheme, which is how his office will operate for the rest of his life. The work runs from 1839 to 1841. It is the first time he is paid to arrange houses rather than plants.
suggested_refs: The rebuilt estate village of Edensor, Chatsworth, 1839-1841

stops.name: Chatsworth, the Great Conservatory finished
stops.date_confidence: attested for the completion in 1840 and the dimensions of roughly 84 by 37 by 19 metres (Chatsworth official history), and for the 1920 demolition after wartime coal shortages killed the collection. The 1962 maze planted inside the surviving perimeter walls is likewise from the Chatsworth account. Some sources give completion as 1841.
stops.campa: The Great Conservatory stands: about eighty-four metres long, thirty-seven wide and nineteen high, the largest glass building in England and the direct rehearsal for everything that comes after it. In the First World War the coal cannot be spared, the collection dies of cold, and in 1920 the structure is pulled down. The perimeter walls are kept. In 1962 a maze is planted inside the empty footprint, so the plan survives at Chatsworth without the building, and a stretch of the original heating tunnel is still walkable underneath.
stops.quote: This remarkable edifice was in fact the parent of the far more famous Crystal Palace.
stops.quote_source: Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton, 1865, reprinted by Bedfordshire Archives
suggested_refs: The maze planted in 1962 inside the surviving walls of the Great Conservatory, Chatsworth
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

stops.name: London, the Gardeners' Chronicle founded
stops.date_confidence: attested as reported: Paxton, the botanist John Lindley, the printer William Bradbury and the journalist and politician Charles Wentworth Dilke founded The Gardeners' Chronicle in 1841 (Wikipedia). No founding document was inspected. Coordinate is a central London pin, the paper's exact first office not established here.
stops.campa: With the botanist John Lindley, the printer William Bradbury and the journalist Charles Wentworth Dilke, Paxton founds The Gardeners' Chronicle. It is a weekly, it makes money, and it gives a gardener a national voice at the moment gardening is being industrialised: cheaper glass after the excise is lifted, cheap iron, cheap coal, and a middle class that wants a conservatory of its own. Paxton holds a share in it and writes for it while still running the gardens at Chatsworth.
suggested_refs: The Gardeners' Chronicle, founded 1841, the trade weekly Paxton co-owned

stops.name: Liverpool, Prince's Park
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1842 commission from Richard Vaughan Yates (Wikipedia; parksandgardens.org). Coordinate corrected: the dossier gave 53.3852, -2.9412, roughly 0.9 km east and outside the park; Princes Park is at approximately 53.386, -2.954.
stops.campa: Richard Vaughan Yates, a Liverpool merchant, pays for a park out of his own pocket and hires Paxton to lay it out: a lake, a carriage drive, a screen of planting, and villa plots round the edge whose ground rents are meant to pay for the whole thing. The landscape raises the value of the land at its border, and the border then pays for the landscape. It is the first English park built on that arithmetic, and the device will be copied for a century. The public walk in it. No public body owns any of it.
suggested_refs: Prince's Park, Liverpool, the speculative residential park of 1842

stops.name: Birkenhead, the People's Garden
stops.date_confidence: attested: designed from 1843 with municipal money, opened 1847, the first publicly financed park in Britain. Frederick Law Olmsted's visit of 3 May 1850 and his later use of it in arguing for American public parks are attested in landscape scholarship and in the atlas file for Olmsted. Coordinate note: the verified pool gives Birkenhead Park at 53.393, -3.041; the pin here is the canonical one already carried in the Olmsted file, retained for map consistency.
stops.campa: Across the Mersey a town commission, not a private patron, votes public money for a public park and gives Paxton the design. He drains the marsh, banks the lakes with the spoil, keeps carriages on a perimeter road and walkers on winding paths below them, and sells the margin as building plots to pay the bill. It is the first publicly financed park in Britain, and Frederick Law Olmsted's case for public parks in America is built on it. It opens in 1847, free to any working man's family in Birkenhead.
suggested_refs: Frederick Law Olmsted's account of the People's Garden at Birkenhead, visited 3 May 1850
Historic England, publication on Birkenhead Park
sources: Historic England, Birkenhead Park publication page

stops.name: Chatsworth, the Emperor Fountain
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1843-1844 construction, the anticipated visit of Tsar Nicholas I that never took place, and the gravity-fed jet advertised as the world's highest (Chatsworth official history; Wikipedia). The Order of St Vladimir conferred on Paxton in 1844 is attested by the Bedfordshire Archives obituary.
stops.campa: Tsar Nicholas I is expected at Chatsworth and the Duke wants something no Russian palace has. Paxton cuts a reservoir into the moor above the house, brings the water down under nothing but its own weight, and throws up a jet advertised as the highest in the world. The Tsar never comes. The Russian Emperor makes Paxton a Knight of the Order of St Vladimir in 1844 all the same. There is no engine anywhere in the works: the jet runs on the weight of the moorland water and nothing else, and it runs still.
suggested_refs: The Emperor Fountain and its moorland reservoir, Chatsworth, 1843-1844
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

stops.name: Coventry, London Road Cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Coventry Cemetery Committee engaged Paxton on 9 October 1845 and the cemetery opened in 1847. Coordinate corrected: the dossier gave 52.3986, -1.5033, about 0.45 km off; the cemetery is at approximately 52.3964, -1.4982.
stops.campa: The Coventry Cemetery Committee engages him on the ninth of October to lay out a burial ground on the London road. Nine years later the same city will send him to Parliament. He designs the ground as a garden: winding walks, specimen planting, a chapel and lodges, the dead set among trees instead of shoulder to shoulder in a parish churchyard that has run out of room. It opens in 1847, one of the earliest municipal cemeteries in England laid out on that principle.
suggested_refs: London Road Cemetery, Coventry, one of the earliest municipal garden cemeteries in England
sources: British History Online, Victoria County History, Warwickshire vol. 8, pp. 248-255

stops.name: London, the Daily News
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Daily News was founded on 21 January 1846 and that Charles Dickens edited it briefly. Reconstruction for the link: Paxton's role as an original proprietor and major investor is drawn from sources outside the atlas record and is not stated in the Dickens file, so it is carried here as reported rather than as document-attested.
stops.campa: A new London morning paper is founded on the twenty-first of January, Liberal, cheap, and built to break the Times. Paxton is among its original proprietors and puts a large sum of his own money into it; Charles Dickens takes the editor's chair, holds it a matter of weeks, and walks away. Paxton sits on the board of the Midland Railway in the same years. His proprietorship of the paper is reported rather than documented; it comes from outside the papers reached for this account.
suggested_refs: The Daily News, founded 21 January 1846, Dickens editing and Paxton among the proprietors
sources: working/journeys/charles_dickens.journey.json, stop naming the Daily News, founded January 1846

stops.name: Chatsworth, the waterlily flowers
stops.date_confidence: attested that Paxton and his Chatsworth staff brought Victoria regia, now Victoria amazonica, into flower in November 1849, and that an image published about then shows his young daughter standing on a floating leaf. Reconstruction for the debunking: the ridge-and-furrow priority rests on the research dossier's synthesis, which could not be re-verified against a single named source. The Conservative Wall date of 1848 is attested by Wikipedia and corrects the dossier's 1838.
stops.campa: The seeds of Victoria regia, the giant Amazonian waterlily, have defeated every glasshouse in England. Paxton builds it a heated tank with a paddle to keep the water turning and brings it into flower in November, the first in the country. An image published at the time shows his young daughter standing upright on one of its floating leaves. He lectures on the ribs beneath that leaf, and the story that they gave him the Crystal Palace is largely his own publicity: the ridge-and-furrow glazing was already at Chatsworth, most recently in the Conservative Wall of 1848.
suggested_refs: The 1849 photograph of Paxton's daughter on a leaf of Victoria regia
The Conservative Wall at Chatsworth, 1848, 331 feet of ridge-and-furrow glass

stops.name: Derby, the sketch on pink blotting paper
stops.date_confidence: the date of 11 June 1850 and the Midland Railway board setting are widely reported in Exhibition histories; the precise room and the full circumstances are not independently documented, and the object usually exhibited as the sketch is catalogued by the Victoria and Albert Museum as a facsimile, accession E.941-1983. That catalogue page could not be loaded directly (403 Forbidden) and is taken from the Art UK record. The presentation on 29 June and the Commission's acceptance on 15 July are reported by the V&A.
stops.campa: He is a director of the Midland Railway and the board is sitting at Derby. The Commission charged with housing the Great Exhibition has months left and no building it can afford to raise. During the meeting Paxton draws on a sheet of pink blotting paper: a long modular shed of iron and glass, one bay repeated down a grid, a ridge and furrow roof, a thing to be made in a factory and bolted together on the ground by men who need not be craftsmen. He presents it on the twenty-ninth of June, and on the fifteenth of July the Commission accepts it.
suggested_refs: Victoria and Albert Museum accession E.941-1983, catalogued as a facsimile of Paxton's original Crystal Palace sketch
sources: Victoria and Albert Museum, 'The Great Exhibition of 1851'
Art UK / V&A object record E.941-1983

stops.name: John Adam Street, the Society of Arts lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested: the lecture 'The Industrial Palace in Hyde-Park' was delivered to the Society of Arts on 13 November 1850, the printed text catalogued by the Royal Commission for the Exhibition of 1851 and transcribed by the Victorian Web. The printed version may carry a reporter's normalisation rather than being a verbatim transcript.
stops.campa: Before the Society of Arts he reads a paper called The Industrial Palace in Hyde-Park and explains the thing in his own voice: standardisation, the twenty-four foot planning grid, glass in one size cut by machine, gutters that drain and carry load at the same time, a building erected by unskilled labour in months because every part of it is the same part as every other. The text survives only as printed, and a printed Victorian lecture carries a reporter's normalising hand. How much of the wording is Paxton's own cannot be settled here.
suggested_refs: Paxton's lecture text, 'The Industrial Palace in Hyde-Park', 13 November 1850, transcribed at victorianweb.org
sources: Royal Commission for the Exhibition of 1851 / Royal Collection Trust catalogue record (albert.rct.uk)

stops.name: Hyde Park, the building rises
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Victoria and Albert Museum's Great Exhibition account for the pane count near 293,655, the daily workforce near 2,000 men and 200 horses, and completion by late January 1851. The length of 1,848 feet and the transept width of about 456 feet are from the same account. Coordinate is the canonical Hyde Park Crystal Palace pin already carried by four other atlas files, inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: Fox, Henderson and Company put up the frame across a site eighteen hundred and forty-eight feet long, widening at the transept to about four hundred and fifty-six. Elms standing in the way are not felled; the transept is arched over the top of them. Some two thousand men and two hundred horses work the ground daily, setting roughly two hundred and ninety-three thousand panes of glass into about four thousand five hundred tons of iron. By late January it is finished. The Exhibition is due to open on the first of May.
suggested_refs: Fox, Henderson and Company's contract drawings for the 1851 Exhibition building
sources: Victoria and Albert Museum, 'The Great Exhibition of 1851'

stops.name: Hyde Park, opening day
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Great Exhibition opened on 1 May 1851 at nine in the morning to season-ticket holders, and over six million admissions were recorded across its run (Victoria and Albert Museum).
stops.campa: At nine in the morning the doors open to season-ticket holders, and the Queen comes to open the Great Exhibition inside a building that did not exist eleven months ago. Paxton is forty-seven. The fountains run indoors. The elms stand inside the transept in full leaf, roofed over rather than felled. Over six million admissions are counted before the Exhibition closes. What the visitors write home about is not the exhibits: it is the light coming through the glass.
suggested_refs: The Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations, opened 1 May 1851
sources: Victoria and Albert Museum, 'The Great Exhibition of 1851'

stops.name: Hyde Park, the closing
stops.date_confidence: attested as 15 October 1851 by Wikipedia's Great Exhibition and Crystal Palace articles; 11 October was the last day open to the public. The research dossier left an 11 versus 15 October discrepancy open on the strength of a V&A page that returns HTTP 404 and therefore supports nothing, so the discrepancy is closed here in favour of 15 October and recorded as closed.
stops.campa: The public are let in for the last time on the eleventh of October, and the formal ceremony closes the Exhibition on the fifteenth. Paxton argues in print for keeping the building where it stands, as a public winter garden for London. Parliament requires its removal from the park, and the Hyde Park ground goes back to grass. Within a year he is buying the building back in pieces, to be carted eight miles south and raised again on a hill above Sydenham.
suggested_refs: Paxton's published argument for retaining the Hyde Park building as a winter garden

stops.name: Windsor Castle, the knighthood
stops.date_confidence: attested by the London Gazette, issue 21257 of 28 October 1851, p. 2812, dateline Windsor Castle, repeated in the Edinburgh Gazette issue 6121 of 31 October. Place corrected: the dossier gave Buckingham Palace at 51.5014, -0.1419, about 37 km wrong. The Gazette gives the notice date rather than a ceremony date; the exact day of the conferral is not established here.
stops.campa: The Gazette carries the notice under a Windsor Castle dateline, four words of formula and a name, and prints his London address as 36 Gloucester Place, Portman Square. He is forty-eight years old. Forty-eight years earlier his father was working another man's fields in Bedfordshire, and the free school at Woburn was the whole of what that family could get for the boy. Nothing about the knighthood changes his employment. He keeps the head gardener's post at Chatsworth and will hold it another seven years.
stops.quote: The Queen was this day pleased to confer the honour of Knighthood upon Joseph Paxton, Esq.
stops.quote_source: The London Gazette, issue 21257, 28 October 1851, p. 2812, dateline Windsor Castle
suggested_refs: London Gazette issue 21257 (28 October 1851) and Edinburgh Gazette issue 6121 (31 October 1851)
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

stops.name: Penge Place, the hill bought
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Crystal Palace Company was formed in 1852, bought the Hyde Park components for about seventy thousand pounds, and acquired the Penge Place site on Sydenham Hill, with Paxton as director and chief designer (Crystal Palace Foundation). The Sydenham building was larger and substantially redesigned rather than a straight reassembly.
stops.campa: A company is formed, the components of the Hyde Park building are bought for about seventy thousand pounds, and ground at Penge Place on Sydenham Hill is acquired to put them on. Paxton is a director of the company and the chief designer of the transfer. The company means to charge admission all year round. What goes up will not be the old building reassembled: it is larger, barrel-vaulted along its whole length, with three transepts where there was one, terraced gardens falling away below it, and waterworks fed from two towers.
suggested_refs: The Crystal Palace Company prospectus and the purchase of the Hyde Park components, 1852
sources: Crystal Palace Foundation, 'History of the Crystal Palace' (crystalpalacefoundation.org.uk)

stops.name: Sydenham, the Palace reopened
stops.date_confidence: attested: the rebuilt and enlarged Crystal Palace opened at Sydenham on 10 June 1854, with decoration by Owen Jones and Matthew Digby Wyatt, prehistoric interpretation under Richard Owen, dinosaur sculptures by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins, and water towers by Isambard Kingdom Brunel.
stops.campa: The Crystal Palace opens on its hill above south London, a permanent commercial attraction now rather than a six-month exhibition. Owen Jones and Matthew Digby Wyatt do the decoration; Richard Owen directs the prehistoric interpretation and Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins builds thirty-three concrete monsters in the grounds below; Isambard Kingdom Brunel designs the water towers. Paxton's name stands over all of it. Inside, the courts run through Egypt, Greece, Rome and the Alhambra. It opens to the public on the tenth of June 1854.
suggested_refs: Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins's dinosaur sculptures, completed 1854 in the Crystal Palace grounds
sources: Crystal Palace Foundation, 'History of the Crystal Palace'

stops.name: Rockhills, the house on the Parade
stops.date_confidence: attested that Rockhills at Sydenham was his later principal residence and the place of his death (Oxford DNB); the sources give only 'the 1850s' for when he took it, and the year here orders the segment. Corrected: the dossier stated he held the Chatsworth appointment for life. He remained head gardener until the sixth Duke died in 1858 and retired then; his widow Sarah remained connected with the estate until her death in 1871. Coordinate approximate, near the historic Rockhills site on Crystal Palace Parade.
stops.campa: He takes a house called Rockhills at the top of Sydenham Hill, a few hundred yards from the Palace, and it becomes his principal residence for the rest of his life. He keeps the Chatsworth appointment until the sixth Duke dies in 1858, then retires from it after thirty-two years in the post. The sources give only the 1850s for when he took the house, so the year here is a placement and not a document. Sarah keeps her connection with the estate and lives on there until 1871.
suggested_refs: Rockhills, Crystal Palace Parade, Paxton's house from the mid-1850s until his death
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Paxton, Sir Joseph' (summary only; full entry paywalled)

segments.name: The Office: Rothschild Houses, the Corps, and the Last Parks

stops.name: Mentmore Towers, the house for a collection
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1850 commission from Baron Mayer Amschel de Rothschild and construction to about 1854, with George Henry Stokes doing much of the detailed design. Date set to 1852 to place the building work; the commission itself is 1850. Coordinate corrected: the dossier gave 51.8749, -0.6392, roughly 3.6 km off; Mentmore Towers is at approximately 51.868, -0.691.
stops.campa: Baron Mayer Amschel de Rothschild wants a house in Buckinghamshire large enough to hold a great art collection, and Paxton designs it with his assistant George Henry Stokes: Jacobean on the outside, plate glass in the windows, hot water heating and forced ventilation throughout, and a central hall roofed in glass. Stokes does much of the drawing, here and on every commission that follows. Building runs from 1850 to about 1854, and the Rothschild collection moves in behind plate glass and warm air.
suggested_refs: Mentmore Towers, Grade I listed, built for Mayer Amschel de Rothschild c. 1850-1854

stops.name: Ferrieres-en-Brie, another Mentmore twice the size
stops.date_confidence: attested that James Mayer de Rothschild commissioned the Chateau de Ferrieres as 'another Mentmore, but twice the size', built c. 1855-1859 by Paxton's office with Stokes on much of the detail. Coordinate corrected: the dossier gave 48.8497, 2.6989, about 3.4 km off; the chateau is at approximately 48.820, 2.712.
stops.campa: James de Rothschild asks for another Mentmore, twice the size, in the park at Ferrieres-en-Brie east of Paris. Paxton's office builds it between about 1855 and 1859, Stokes again doing much of the detailed design. An English gardener is exporting a French chateau into France. He is by this point a Member of Parliament and a company director, he has not held a spade professionally in thirty years, and the drawing is done by other men in an office with his name on the door.
suggested_refs: Chateau de Ferrieres, built for James Mayer de Rothschild, c. 1855-1859

stops.name: Matlock, the rifle volunteers
stops.date_confidence: attested for 17 March 1860, when Paxton raised and became captain of the 11th Derbyshire (Matlock) Rifle Volunteer Corps within the national home-defence volunteer movement (Wikipedia). No combat service; the role is civic and magisterial.
stops.campa: Invasion from France is expected and the country raises rifle volunteer corps by the hundred. Paxton raises the eleventh Derbyshire, at Matlock, and takes command of it as captain. It is a magistrate's function rather than a soldier's: drill nights, target practice, a subscription list. No call to service ever comes. He is fifty-six, and the hillsides his men drill on are the ones where he spent thirty years planting conifers and running pipes of hot water underneath glass.
suggested_refs: The 11th Derbyshire (Matlock) Rifle Volunteer Corps, raised 17 March 1860

stops.name: Dundee, Baxter Park
stops.date_confidence: attested that Paxton designed Baxter Park, Dundee, in 1863 (Wikipedia). Honest gap: the research pool supplies no coordinate for this stop, and the pin here is an approximate placement on Baxter Park itself rather than a figure taken from a source.
stops.campa: Dundee gets a public park and Paxton designs it, one of the last landscapes he lays out. Broad walks, an open green wide enough for the whole town to gather on, a pavilion set on the high ground looking north over the mills. Twenty-one years after Prince's Park the idea has stopped being an experiment: a manufacturing city buys ground the mills do not own and has a gardener out of Bedfordshire draw the paths across it. He is sixty years old when it opens.
suggested_refs: Baxter Park, Dundee, laid out to Paxton's design and opened 1863

stops.name: Coventry, returned unopposed
stops.date_confidence: attested: elected unopposed as Liberal member for Coventry on 2 December 1854, returned again in 1857 and 1859, and holding the seat until his death (Bedfordshire Archives obituary; Hansard historic person record).
stops.campa: The city whose cemetery he designed returns him to the House of Commons at a by-election, unopposed, as a Liberal. He is fifty-one and has never stood for anything before. He is returned again in 1857 and 1859 and holds the seat until he dies, speaking for the weavers in the House down to his last session. Coventry lives by ribbon-weaving, a trade about to be broken by free trade with France, and its member is a knight who builds glasshouses for dukes and country houses for bankers.
suggested_refs: Hansard historic person record, 'Sir Joseph Paxton', api.parliament.uk
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

stops.name: Westminster, the huts that were not built
stops.date_confidence: attested and verified verbatim: Hansard, HC Deb 5 March 1855 vol 137, 'Ordnance Estimates, Supply'. Hansard's speaker label is SIR JOSEPH PAXTON, and the report is in nineteenth-century third-person indirect style, so the quoted words sit inside reported speech rather than standing as direct address.
stops.campa: The army in the Crimea is dying of exposure and the Commons is going through the Ordnance estimates. Paxton stands up as a contractor rather than as a politician and takes the timetable apart: nothing done on the ground, no tender out before the twenty-second of January, then huts for twenty thousand men promised complete by the fifteenth of March. There was not, he says, enough wood of that description in Great Britain to erect one half of them. He wants departments to do as little as they can avoid out of their own offices and to take plans and estimates by tender.
stops.quote: Not even a tender was sent out before the 22nd of January, and then a tender was sent out for the erection of huts capable of accommodating 20,000 men, which huts were to be completed by the 15th of March.
stops.quote_source: Hansard, HC Deb 5 March 1855 vol 137, 'Ordnance Estimates, Supply'; initial word capitalised for the excerpt
suggested_refs: Hansard, HC Deb 5 March 1855 vol 137, the Aldershot hut contracts
sources: Hansard, HC Deb 5 March 1855 vol 137, 'Ordnance Estimates, Supply' (api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard)

stops.name: Westminster, the Great Victorian Way
stops.date_confidence: attested that Paxton laid a Great Victorian Way scheme, a glass-roofed circulation loop of some ten or eleven miles round central London, before a select committee in June 1855, and that it was never built. The quoted description is from the 1865 obituary, not from Paxton's own submission. Day set to 01.
stops.campa: He lays before a select committee a scheme for a glass-roofed circuit around central London, ten or eleven miles of it, an arcade on the model of the Crystal Palace transept with railways worked on the atmospheric principle running inside it and houses and shops along its length. It would cost a large fraction of a national budget. The committee considers it seriously. Nothing whatever is built, and the scheme survives in the select committee's papers and in the description his obituary gives it fifteen years later.
stops.quote: A magnificent arcade, resembling the transept of the old Crystal Palace, in which were to be included lines of railway worked on the atmospheric principle, and bordered by handsome dwellings and shops.
stops.quote_source: Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton, 1865, reprinted by Bedfordshire Archives, describing the 1855 Great Victorian Way
suggested_refs: The select committee papers on the Great Victorian Way, 1855
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'

stops.name: Westminster, the price of a glasshouse at Kew
stops.date_confidence: attested and verified against Hansard, 'Supply, Civil Service Estimates', 18 July 1859. Corrected: the research dossier put the forty thousand geraniums in Paxton's mouth. They were raised later in the same debate by Mr Kinnaird, taking up Paxton's line; Paxton's own contribution is confined to the cost of covering ground with glass.
stops.campa: The Civil Service estimates carry twenty-five thousand pounds for a new glasshouse at Kew, and the member for Coventry, who has covered more ground with glass than anyone alive, tells the House the figure is twice what it needs to be. An acre can be roofed for ten thousand, he says, so half the sum asked would be amply sufficient. Later in the same debate Mr Kinnaird raises the forty thousand geraniums being potted at the public expense, a complaint often put into Paxton's mouth afterwards and not his.
stops.quote: an acre of ground might very well be covered with glass for the sum of £10,000, and he therefore was of opinion that half the amount which was asked for would be amply sufficient
stops.quote_source: Hansard, HC Deb 18 July 1859, 'Supply, Civil Service Estimates'
suggested_refs: Hansard, HC Deb 18 July 1859, the Kew glasshouse estimate
sources: Hansard, HC Deb 18 July 1859, 'Supply, Civil Service Estimates' (hansard.parliament.uk)

stops.name: Westminster, the last speech, on the weavers
stops.date_confidence: attested as his last identified Hansard contribution, HC Deb 30 June 1864 vol 176, 'Observations', on the depressed Coventry ribbon trade. Reported in Hansard's third-person indirect style; the quoted words sit inside that reporting.
stops.campa: His last recorded contribution is about Coventry. The ribbon trade is ruined, the French commercial treaty having come into force at the exact moment the trade was already deep in depression, and he tells the House that he can bear witness to the distress himself, that it existed and still exists. He speaks of the marvellous patience and forbearance with which the weavers have borne their sufferings. He does not speak in the House again. Eleven months later he is dead.
stops.quote: He was unfortunately able to bear testimony to the severe distress which had existed, and still existed, in Coventry.
suggested_refs: Hansard, HC Deb 30 June 1864 vol 176, on the Coventry ribbon trade

stops.name: Rockhills, the death at Sydenham
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, place and age of sixty-one (Bedfordshire Archives obituary; Oxford DNB). Reported rather than documented: the collapse earlier in the year described by biographers as probably a heart attack, the Gladstones among his final visitors, and the probate valuation of just under one hundred and eighty thousand pounds, all from the Oxford DNB entry, whose full text is paywalled.
stops.campa: He dies at Rockhills on the eighth of June, sixty-one years old, after a collapse earlier in the year that his biographers take for a heart attack. William and Catherine Gladstone are reported among his last visitors. Probate values his personal estate at just under a hundred and eighty thousand pounds. He had retired from Chatsworth seven years before and had gone on designing parks regardless; Baxter Park is two years old. Down the hill from the windows of the house the Palace he moved here fills the whole sky.
suggested_refs: The probate record of Sir Joseph Paxton, 1865
sources: Bedfordshire Archives, 'Obituary of Sir Joseph Paxton'
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Paxton, Sir Joseph' (summary only; full entry paywalled)

stops.name: Edensor, St Peter's churchyard
stops.date_confidence: the burial place is attested by Wikipedia, which states he was buried on the Chatsworth estate in St Peter's churchyard, Edensor. The burial date of 15 June 1865 appears in no reachable source and rests on the paywalled Oxford DNB; it is carried here on that authority alone. Coordinate corrected: the dossier gave 53.2247, -1.6154 and the afterlife pool gave 53.2276, -1.6076, which is Chatsworth House itself; St Peter's churchyard is at approximately 53.2272, -1.6255.
stops.campa: He is buried in the churchyard at Edensor, the village he rebuilt, on the estate he ran for thirty-two years, among the graves of the Cavendishes he worked for. The church standing over him now is not the one he knew: George Gilbert Scott rebuilds St Peter's two years after the funeral. The date of the fifteenth of June rests on a reference work not directly reachable, and the place is not in any doubt. Sarah stays on the estate another six years.
suggested_refs: St Peter's Church, Edensor, rebuilt by George Gilbert Scott in 1867 over the churchyard holding Paxton's grave

stops.name: London Road Cemetery, the memorial
stops.date_confidence: attested that a memorial to Paxton by Joseph Goddard was erected in 1868 in London Road Cemetery, Coventry, and that a bust by William F. Woodington was unveiled in Crystal Palace Park in 1873. Note: Wikipedia's cemetery article describes Goddard as an architect rather than a sculptor. Coordinate corrected: the research pool pinned this memorial to Coventry city centre, 1.9 km from the cemetery it stands in.
stops.campa: Three years after his death Coventry raises a memorial to him inside the cemetery he designed and the constituency he represented. Five years after that a bust by William Woodington is set up in Crystal Palace Park, overlooking the central walk; he has been dead eight years by then. Neither monument stands at Chatsworth. The Coventry memorial is the work of Joseph Goddard, whom one reference article calls an architect and another a sculptor, and which he was is not settled here.
suggested_refs: Joseph Goddard's 1868 Paxton memorial, London Road Cemetery, Coventry
William F. Woodington's 1873 bust of Paxton, Crystal Palace Park

stops.name: Crystal Palace Park, the fire
stops.date_confidence: attested for the destruction of the Sydenham building by fire on 30 November 1936, the estimated crowd of a hundred thousand, Churchill's reported remark, the survival of the two water towers and part of the north nave, and the demolition of the north tower by explosives in 1941 (Wikipedia). The cause was never conclusively established; the accidental cloakroom fire is the standard account, and later rumours of arson have no evidentiary support.
stops.campa: On the night of the thirtieth of November the Sydenham Palace burns. An estimated hundred thousand people come up the hill to watch it go, Winston Churchill among them, reported as saying this is the end of an age. The cause is never conclusively established and an accidental cloakroom fire is the standard account. Two water towers and a damaged section of the north nave survive the night; the north tower is brought down with explosives in 1941. Paxton has been dead seventy-one years.
suggested_refs: The Crystal Palace Museum, Anerley Hill, in the former School of Practical Engineering building
sources: Crystal Palace Foundation, 'History of the Crystal Palace'
